Sci-Arc “Changing Concepts” poster

April Greiman’s lecture-series poster for the Southern California Institute of Architecture: pixel type in black squares, dot-screen gradients, and a spaced-out subtitle.

Source
V&A: Sci-Arc, E.1500-2010
Creator
April Greiman
Made

Style
New Wave typography (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods

Inspected the V&A photograph of object E.1500-2010 (image 2011EN9653, 1200 × 1600) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored. The smallest text is not readable at this size.

Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A holds the poster as E.1500-2010, colour offset lithograph, 91.5 × 61 cm, published in the United States in 1986, and describes it as the “Sci-Arc Changing Concepts poster”. V&A E.1500-2010.

Observed

  • Overlapping rectangles in orange, magenta, pale yellow, and cyan fade into each other as gradients.
  • A white dotted drawing of a Vitruvian figure in a circle and square fills a panel that is covered by a regular grid of dots.
  • A small orange-framed photograph of broken classical fragments sits at the centre.
  • “sci-arc” is set in blocky pixel letters, one letter on each black square, with wide gaps between the squares.
  • “changing / concepts of s p a c e / in architecture / and art” is set flush left in lines that change weight, and “space” is spaced out letter by letter.
  • A lecture list at the top right runs on thin rules, with black numbered squares and black bars at the right edge.
  • A column of small photographs runs down the left edge. Fields of scattered dots cover the orange ground.

Why it belongs

The poster keeps the Basel habits (steps, bars, screens, spacing) and replaces film halftones with computer dot patterns and bitmap letters. It sits at the point where New Wave turns into digital design.

The pixel letters are clean, not distressed, so the counter-rule on damaged letterforms still holds.

Borrow

Set a short name one letter per solid square, with gaps between the squares.

Letterspace only one word in a phrase to make it the subject.

Put a list on hairline rules and end each row with a black bar at the page edge.
